prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Whether primary schools should go on teaching joined-up handwriting is usually argued as a contest between the past and the future, with the pen cast as a relic and the keyboard as the plain destination of every child now in Reception, but that framing hides what is actually at stake, which is whether children leave primary school able to write by hand quickly and legibly for long stretches, and on that question I will argue that teaching a joined hand remains the most dependable route to that ability and that schools which drop it will be taking something from pupils that they cannot easily get back later.

It helps to begin with what handwriting is for in a school, because the answer is less sentimental than defenders of cursive tend to make it sound. Every child in England will sit written examinations at sixteen and again at eighteen, and the great majority of those papers are answered by hand, under time pressure, for an examiner who has to be able to read the result. A pupil whose writing is slow or hard to decipher pays for it in marks without anyone noticing until the scripts come back, and the research on handwriting fluency, much of it associated with Steve Graham and his collaborators in the United States, has found again and again that children who form letters automatically write longer and better organised texts, because the effort of making the letters no longer competes with the effort of deciding what to say. Anything that raises automaticity is therefore working for composition and spelling and thought as well as for tidiness, and the real question about joining is whether it raises automaticity or merely decorates it.

The honest answer is that the evidence for cursive over printed letters as such is thinner than its champions claim. Comparisons between the two scripts have mostly found small differences, and the more excited assertions, that cursive rewires the brain for literacy or cures dyslexia, run well ahead of anything that has been shown. What survives scrutiny is narrower and still sufficient for the argument: writing letters by hand, as against typing them, appears to help young children learn to recognise them, with imaging work by Karin James and colleagues finding that pre-literate children who drew letters freehand showed more activity in reading-related regions of the brain than children who typed or traced the same letters, and a joined hand is a way of making that practised movement continuous. The case for joining proper rests on something more ordinary, which is speed. When the pen stays on the paper through a whole word, the hand makes fewer lifts and fewer restarts, and a child who has been taught consistent entry and exit strokes can write a word as a single gesture instead of a string of separate letters. That also turns the word into a unit of spelling in the hand as well as in the head, so that a child who has rehearsed the movement for the ending of "walking" or "station" has practised a spelling pattern as a pattern.

The strongest objection is about time. Adults, the objection runs, seldom write anything longer than a shopping list or a signature on a screen, and the hours spent on loops and joins would be better spent on keyboard skills that children will use for the rest of their lives. I take this seriously and I think it fails on an asymmetry between the two skills. Handwriting has to be learned while the small muscles of the hand and the habits of grip and letter formation are still being set, and a child who reaches Year 7 starting every circle in the wrong place and gripping the pen in a fist will very likely carry that into adulthood, because bad habits in movement are far harder to unlearn than they were to acquire. Touch typing has no such window. A nine or ten year old who can already read and spell fluently can learn to type properly in a matter of months of regular practice, and an adult can learn it in an evening class, so that the sensible order is to teach by hand while it can only be taught early and to teach the keyboard when it can be taught at any time. Nor does handwriting practice consume the hours its critics imagine, since in a well run classroom it is a few short sessions a week, folded into the same lessons that teach phonics and spelling.

There is also the matter of reading, which gets forgotten in arguments that concentrate on production. A great deal of the written record that matters to a family or a country is in joined script, from grandparents' letters to the marginal comments a teacher leaves on a page of work to the archives that historians and genealogists use, and a person who has never been taught to join letters finds a handwritten sentence from a century ago close to a foreign script. Reading cursive takes far less teaching than writing it, but it is learned most naturally by those who have formed the letters themselves. Several American states, having let cursive fall out of the curriculum when the Common Core standards left it out, have since passed laws to put it back, partly because teachers found that students could not read the documents they were being asked to study in the original, and I count that as a small natural experiment whose result was reversed within a decade.

Against all this stand the children for whom joined writing is genuinely difficult, and any honest defence has to deal with them. Some pupils have dyslexia or dysgraphia or a motor difficulty, some are left-handed and smear their work as the hand passes over it, and some simply find that the diagonal join from one letter to the next makes their writing worse. Specialists disagree about whether cursive helps or hinders children with dyslexia, which suggests that nobody should be dogmatic about individual cases, and the national curriculum for England is already sensible on the point, asking pupils in the later primary years to understand which letters are best left unjoined. What follows from that is a case for teaching joining with a light hand, starting once letters are secure at around seven, expecting a personal hybrid style to emerge by the end of primary school, marking for legibility and speed rather than for conformity to a copybook, and giving a keyboard without stigma to the child who really cannot manage a pen. Each of these is an argument about how to teach, and none of them supports abandoning the teaching.

The equity argument seems to me the most important, and the one that proponents of dropping joined writing are least likely to raise. A child from a home with pens, paper, letters on the mantelpiece and adults who write things down will pick up some version of a fluent hand whatever the school does. A child from a home where none of that is routine has only school to learn from, and if the school treats handwriting as optional the child who needed it taught is the one who goes without. We know how this tends to run, because skills that are left to families to hand on become markers of the families they came from, and a fluent legible hand in a written exam is a small piece of advantage that costs a school very little to distribute widely.

I should say what would change my mind, since an argument of this kind ought to name its own limit. If public examinations moved to keyboards for everyone, which some countries and some awarding bodies are already moving towards, then the main practical reason for demanding sustained handwriting at speed would weaken considerably, and what would remain is the case from letter learning, from the reading of old documents, and from the habits of mind that go with writing by hand. Those are real but lighter, and in that world I would still teach joining, though more briefly and with less insistence. That world has not arrived. Students in England still write for hours in exam halls, and they will go on doing so for as long as the people who set the papers believe that handwriting is a fair way to test what a young person knows, which in a time of anxiety about machine-written work they have every reason to go on believing.

So my position is that primary schools should keep teaching joined-up writing, should teach it from the age when the hand is ready, and should do so with enough flexibility that a child who ends up with a clear, quick, half-joined script of their own counts as a success and not a failure. The pen will not vanish from children's lives in the next ten years, nor will the need to take notes in a meeting without a laptop, to fill in a form at a counter, to write a card, or to read what someone else wrote by hand. A child who leaves primary school able to do these things comfortably has been given a modest tool that will serve across a lifetime, and the cost of giving it is a few short lessons a week for a few years, which is a price worth paying for something that cannot be taught as easily later.
